video_title: From Harvard at 18 to Building Lighter
gist: Vlad Novakoski, founder of the ZK perpetuals exchange Lighter, traces a career arc from math/physics/informatics Olympiads to Citadel, Quora, Adapar and Lunch Club, and explains why he pivoted a networking startup into a decentralized derivatives venue. The investor-relevant content is less about Lighter's token than about repeatable alpha mechanisms: sourcing talent from Olympiad cohorts before institutions caught on, alpha decay after 2008, why the scientific establishment called neural nets a dead end, and why he thinks ZK proofs are crypto's transformer moment and TradFi will adopt from the margins (ICE/Polymarket) rather than by wholesale replacement.

insights.claim: Vlad Novakoski describes Olympiad-derived talent as 'undiscovered alpha' that has now been arbitraged away: when he joined Citadel around 2004-2005, even that firm's elite recruiting team had never heard of the math/physics/informatics Olympiads, whereas today essentially every top quant firm recruits from that exact pool.
insights.speaker: Vlad Novakoski
insights.so_what: Talent-sourcing edges decay like trading edges — investors backing 'we hire from X pipeline' theses should check whether the pipeline is already institutionally priced.
insights.quote: It was more of like just like undiscovered alpha, right?

insights.claim: The competitive-exam talent edge took years to diffuse because it spread person-by-person through insiders (an early Jane Street Olympiad alum, HRT, the CTO of Facebook, Google's first CTO) rather than through any institutional recruiting channel.
insights.speaker: Vlad Novakoski
insights.so_what: Slow, relationship-mediated diffusion is why non-consensus talent or data sources can stay mispriced for a decade — look for edges that only travel by word of mouth.
insights.quote: and then the alpha got got squeezed out.

insights.claim: Novakoski's contribution at Adapar was persuading its recruiting team to source interns specifically from Olympiad cohorts (legal to hire at 17), and that pipeline produced co-founders of Cognition (Scott Wu, also his Lunch Club co-founder), Scale, Perplexity and Modal, plus crypto founders and quant-firm hires.
insights.speaker: Vlad Novakoski
insights.so_what: Concentrating young elite talent in one building generated more enterprise value through their later startups than through the host company — an argument for angel exposure to alumni networks of talent-dense firms.
insights.quote: What was new that I brought to the table was that we should source them from the Olympians.

insights.claim: Novakoski's model for spotting future outliers is rank-order persistence: stack-rank a national talent cohort and the ordering barely changes year to year, so projecting it 20 years forward identifies who will contribute.
insights.speaker: Vlad Novakoski
insights.so_what: A cheap heuristic for early-stage founder screening: persistence of relative ranking within a measurable domain, not absolute achievement at a point in time.
insights.quote: that ranking doesn't change that much from one year to the next if you I thought okay well if you project that out 20 years it's probably going to not about the same then.

insights.claim: The base rate for elite competitive-programming cohorts producing extreme outcomes is high and predates the internet era: of the three-person Harvard team sent to the 1993 ICPC, two became billionaires.
insights.speaker: Vlad Novakoski
insights.so_what: Supports treating small, extremely selective technical cohorts as a persistent (if now crowded) source of outlier founders rather than a one-off 2000s artifact.
insights.quote: So out of that three person team, not one but two became billionaires.

themes.theme: Alpha Decay and the Post-2008 Quant Break

insights.claim: Ken Griffin personally told Novakoski that the dorm-room strategies he had backtested successfully no longer worked because Citadel had already arbitraged them away — a live example of backtest-versus-live divergence caused by a specific competitor rather than by data-mining error.
insights.speaker: Vlad Novakoski
insights.so_what: A clean reminder that a strong backtest with near-zero live PnL usually means someone larger got there first, not that the model is broken.
insights.quote: I think I found them like five, six years too late. But yes, cuz I had some good back tests, but in in real trading, it was like close to zero.

insights.claim: Novakoski dates a structural break in quant trading to 2008: before it, simple strategies plus fast execution (what became HFT) worked, and after it those simple strategies stopped working, forcing quant desks into machine learning to find more complicated market patterns.
insights.speaker: Vlad Novakoski
insights.so_what: Frames ML in finance as a necessity born of edge exhaustion rather than a fad — and implies latency-only strategies have been structurally impaired for over 15 years.
insights.quote: after 2008 those simple strategies stopped working and you had to find more complicated patterns in the market.

insights.claim: Griffin's pitch to Novakoski was that alpha discovery is a team sport because markets are near-efficient, so an inefficiency requires several independent conditions to be true simultaneously and combinations are easier to find in a group with diverse backgrounds.
insights.speaker: Vlad Novakoski
insights.so_what: Argues structurally against solo-quant and single-signal research shops; multi-disciplinary research teams should out-discover individuals as markets get more efficient.
insights.quote: the markets are very close to being efficient and so like to find in efficiencies like a bunch of different things all have to be true and it's like easier to find those combinations in a group.

insights.claim: Disclosure incentives run in opposite directions in tech and quant finance: tech firms publicize any interesting technique to create buzz, while quant firms actively want competitors to believe their models are basic, meaning public sophistication signals are systematically misleading in trading.
insights.speaker: Vlad Novakoski
insights.so_what: Do not infer a trading firm's capability from its publications or marketing — the absence of signal is deliberate and the true adoption curve of ML in finance ran far earlier than the public record suggests.
insights.quote: you keep a secret and you want the competitors to think that you're doing something very basic even if you're not

insights.claim: Adapar's founding premise, per Novakoski, is that much of the 2008 risk miscalculation was a data-aggregation failure — the data that should have been in one place wasn't — rather than a pure modeling failure.
insights.speaker: Vlad Novakoski
insights.so_what: Positions portfolio-data consolidation as risk infrastructure, not reporting software — relevant to valuing wealth-tech and risk-aggregation businesses.
insights.quote: if you look at 2008 a lot of the reason why risk was miscalculated is A lot of the data that should have been there in one place wasn't.

insights.claim: Novakoski argues most allocators do not actually know their own exposures because ownership is layered — the same name can be held directly, inside an SPV, and inside a mutual fund — making true correlations non-obvious even to the owner.
insights.speaker: Vlad Novakoski
insights.so_what: Hidden look-through concentration is a live tail risk for multi-vehicle portfolios; look-through exposure tooling is the prerequisite to any AI-driven allocation advice.
insights.quote: maybe somebody owns Apple stock directly, but they also own an SPV. They may also own a mutual fund that has Apple. Like under like the the correlations are actually not obvious.

insights.claim: When Novakoski placed 12th in the Intel Science Talent Search with an optics-based neural network project, the Nobel laureates and scientific establishment judging it told him neural networks were a dead end and that serious science meant quantum — and he redirected away from the field for roughly 12 years as a result.
insights.speaker: Vlad Novakoski
insights.so_what: The most credentialed consensus in a field can be catastrophically wrong about which technology compounds — a caution against deferring to establishment opinion on frontier-technology allocation.
insights.quote: Yeah, all this like machine learning stuff, like that's a dead end. Like you like it's kind of it's cute that you did this work as a kid, but like if you want to do science, like do quantum

insights.claim: Novakoski qualifies the neural-network dismissal as defensible at the time because it predated internet-scale data — the bottleneck was data availability, not algorithmic insight, which is why the same ideas worked a decade later.
insights.speaker: Vlad Novakoski
insights.so_what: A reusable test for 'failed' technologies: ask whether the binding constraint was the idea or a missing input that a later secular trend supplies.

insights.claim: Novakoski says Quora had the ingredients to build the first good LLM — dense, information-rich text data, unlike Spotify's or Netflix's recommendation datasets — but language models 12 years ago added no alpha to Quora's prediction models, so the opportunity went unbuilt.
insights.speaker: Vlad Novakoski
insights.so_what: Owning the right proprietary corpus is necessary but not sufficient — timing against model capability determines whether data assets convert into value.
insights.quote: Like in principle, we could have built the first good LLM.

insights.claim: Novakoski's first conviction that generative AI had consumer product-market fit came in late 2021, roughly a year before ChatGPT, from an anecdotal signal: his interns said they no longer did homework because GPT-2-class models were good enough.
insights.speaker: Vlad Novakoski
insights.so_what: Behavioral usage signals from young power users led the market's repricing of AI by about a year — a template for sourcing early PMF evidence before it shows in revenue.
insights.quote: in late 2021 I remember some of our interns were like you know we don't really do homework anymore

insights.claim: When Dario presented OpenAI's work to Novakoski's startup community (South Park Commons) in 2018, the pitch was competing with DeepMind on video games, and LLMs were a two-person side effort that was not the company's main thing.
insights.speaker: Vlad Novakoski
insights.so_what: The eventual franchise line inside a frontier lab was a minority internal bet — argues for valuing labs on option value across research lines rather than on the headline program.
insights.quote: They had like two guys on their team who were doing this LLM stuff. like even with an open that wasn't their main thing

insights.claim: Novakoski maintains that his teenage photonics project — running neural networks with optics instead of silicon chips — is still relevant today, and that optical computing is a genuinely new form of computing alongside quantum.
insights.speaker: Vlad Novakoski
insights.so_what: A named alternative-compute vector from someone who worked on it decades early; relevant to anyone sizing non-GPU compute exposure.
insights.quote: the idea of using optics instead of silicon is a thing and I think is like that is a new form of computing as is you know quantum

insights.claim: The market gap Lighter was built for is that digital assets representing decentralized protocols were overwhelmingly traded off their own rails — when Lighter started, on-chain venues such as AMMs accounted for less than 1% of digital-asset trading volume.
insights.speaker: Vlad Novakoski
insights.so_what: Quantifies the addressable share shift on-chain venues are attacking; the migration of that volume is the single number to track for the DEX-perp thesis.
insights.quote: for the most part like that was less than 1% of the volume

insights.claim: Novakoski defines Lighter against five simultaneous pillars — low cost, low latency, secure, verifiable, composable — arguing the prior frontier forced a trade-off among them and Lighter's contribution is achieving them together.
insights.speaker: Vlad Novakoski
insights.so_what: A concrete scorecard for evaluating any competing decentralized derivatives venue: which of the five pillars it actually delivers versus trades away.
insights.quote: these like five um pillars right like low cost, low latency, secure, verifiable, composable.

insights.claim: Novakoski separates verifiability from security as distinct properties, arguing verifiability is what would have prevented Madoff and FTX while security addresses hacks and asset seizure.
insights.speaker: Vlad Novakoski
insights.so_what: Reframes exchange due diligence: custody safety and provable solvency are different risks, and most venues only address one.
insights.quote: with verifiability, you wouldn't have made off, you wouldn't have, you know, FTX, you wouldn't have a lot of these things that have been a problem for for finance.

insights.claim: Novakoski frames ZK proofs as crypto's equivalent of the transformer in AI — a once-in-a-generation technology that improves multiple dimensions at once instead of forcing the usual optimize-X-at-the-expense-of-Y trade-off.
insights.speaker: Vlad Novakoski
insights.so_what: If correct, ZK is an infrastructure-layer regime change rather than a feature, and venues not built on it face a structural rather than incremental disadvantage.
insights.quote: I think in AI like the transformer was such thing, right? I think in in crypto the ZK proofs were such a thing where like with this technology you can actually like do better across many dimensions relative to the previous frontier.

insights.claim: Novakoski claims Lighter is currently the biggest ZK project and that it is arguably what proves ZK has real applications, tying the credibility of the whole ZK category to Lighter's traction.
insights.speaker: Vlad Novakoski
insights.so_what: Creates a reflexive link: Lighter's volume growth is the main live evidence for ZK utility, so its stumble would drag sentiment across ZK-adjacent assets.
insights.quote: And I think right now we're the biggest ZK project. Like I think arguably like lighter is kind of what proves that there's um that ZK has real applications.

insights.claim: Lighter's core technology took 18 months of heads-down engineering before any public launch because a low-latency, low-cost, secure, verifiable and composable exchange had never been built, and the team used ZK in novel ways to do it.
insights.speaker: Vlad Novakoski
insights.so_what: An 18-month unpublicized build is a real barrier to entry — fast-follower competitors face a long lead time, not a fork.

insights.claim: Novakoski argues the genuinely new form of composability is not software-level DeFi composability, which already existed, but balance-sheet-level composability where tokenized stocks, perpetuals and options sit on the same balance sheet.
insights.speaker: Vlad Novakoski
insights.so_what: Cross-margining across tokenized equities and crypto derivatives is the capital-efficiency unlock that could pull TradFi flow on-chain — watch which venues ship unified margin first.
insights.quote: now we're talking about like tokenized stocks and and pers and options all in the same balance sheet

insights.claim: Lighter is pursuing a simultaneous product-and-infrastructure strategy: Lighter Core is interoperable with other Lighter instances run by partners including Telegram Wallet and Robin Hood, with more partners to come, while the team also ships direct products like options and AI-agent features.
insights.speaker: Vlad Novakoski
insights.so_what: White-label distribution through consumer front-ends is the growth vector to monitor; named partners give a concrete checklist for verifying traction.
insights.quote: lighter core is interoperable with other instances of lighter that were um that are um used by partners like telegram wallet Robin Hood etc.

insights.claim: Lighter emerged from an internal competition — the team ran what Novakoski calls an internal YC, testing three ideas in parallel and merging useful parts of the losers into the winner, rather than announcing a top-down pivot.
insights.speaker: Vlad Novakoski
insights.so_what: A transferable process for evaluating whether a portfolio company's pivot preserves or destroys team capital.
insights.quote: It was more like let's run kind of like an internal YC within our company and let best idea win.

insights.claim: The participatory pivot process let Lunch Club retain 80% of its engineering team through the transition into Lighter, which Novakoski treats as the reason the pivot succeeded where starting from scratch would have failed.
insights.speaker: Vlad Novakoski
insights.so_what: Engineering retention through a pivot is a hard diligence metric that distinguishes a real pivot from a disguised restart.
insights.quote: So we were able to retain 80% of our engineering team through the pivot.

insights.claim: Novakoski pushes back on prevailing anti-VC sentiment in crypto, arguing the 2022 pivot was only possible because existing VCs funded it during a window when markets were weak across every industry — after the earlier crypto collapse and before AI picked up — with Robin Hood, SaaS names and Coinbase all sharply down.
insights.speaker: Vlad Novakoski
insights.so_what: Patient venture capital is the option value that lets teams re-underwrite ideas in a drawdown — a point against pure token-only funding structures.
insights.quote: this was in 2022 when the markets were weak across pretty much every industry. It was right after the collapse of kind of earlier crypto even before AI started to pick up.

insights.claim: Founders Fund, whose Peter Thiel connection Novakoski made years earlier through the Facebook CTO, co-led Lighter's last venture round before the token launch.
insights.speaker: Vlad Novakoski
insights.so_what: Identifies the marquee pre-token cap-table anchor — relevant to unlock schedules and to reading the signalling value of the round.
insights.quote: the last venture round we we did before launching a token you know they co-led that one

insights.claim: Lighter's quiet 18-month build was paired with private prototype demos to traders at conferences, so that at launch it had 100 traders who already knew the team and committed to months of testing rather than five-minute trials.
insights.speaker: Vlad Novakoski
insights.so_what: Pre-seeded professional liquidity at launch is the difference between a cold-start DEX and one with immediate depth — a diligence question for any new venue.
insights.quote: when we did have the tech ready, we had 100 traders ready to try it.

insights.claim: Novakoski argues TradFi will never swap out core infrastructure on a better-mousetrap pitch — institutions running trillions in volume over 150 years will tell you to go build it first and prove it — so adoption comes only after visible product-market fit outside their core.
insights.speaker: Vlad Novakoski
insights.so_what: Sets expectations for the timeline of institutional on-chain adoption: proof first, integration later, so headline partnership announcements should be discounted.
insights.quote: you're running trillions of dollars of you know volumes and you've done it for 150 years but I have a better way you switch to my like it doesn't work

insights.claim: Novakoski points to ICE's strategic investment in Polymarket as the template for institutional entry — incumbents test new technology in a genuinely new space (prediction markets) they weren't already operating in, then expand if it works.
insights.speaker: Vlad Novakoski
insights.so_what: Predicts where the next exchange-operator investments land: greenfield product categories, not replacements of existing matching engines.
insights.quote: I think the uh example of um you know ICE making a strategic investment poly market is like a good example of this right

insights.claim: Novakoski draws an explicit analogy to enterprise AI adoption: large banks did not decide in 2023 to rebuild everything with AI, they trialled it pocket by pocket across business lines until it became the default — and crypto rails will follow the same margin-inward path.
insights.speaker: Vlad Novakoski
insights.so_what: Adoption revenue arrives as a slow ramp across many small deployments, not a step-change contract — model institutional crypto revenue accordingly.
insights.quote: it's not like large banks in 2023 said okay this AI stuff is interesting we're going to rebuild everything with it right now

insights.claim: Novakoski states Lighter's long-term mission as being the technology layer for the merge of DeFi and TradFi, explicitly declining to define a five-year plan and instead planning one to two quarters out while listening to customers.
insights.speaker: Vlad Novakoski
insights.so_what: The stated end-state is infrastructure rent from converged markets, not exchange fee share — which is a different and larger TAM if it lands.
insights.quote: whatever the merge of DeFi and Strati looks like, we want to build the tech to make it happen.

insights.claim: The Bankless host frames Lighter as a third-generation exchange — after centralized venues like Coinbase, Kraken and Binance and after AMMs like Uniswap — because ZK circuits deliver auditability the CEXs cannot and latency the AMMs cannot, and argues NASDAQ, CME and NYSE should eventually sit on the same ZK substrate.
insights.speaker: host (Bankless)
insights.so_what: Articulates the maximal bull case for ZK exchange infrastructure and the incumbents it would eventually disintermediate.
insights.quote: Seems like lighter is like something like Gen 3 or the the most latest generation of exchange technology

insights.claim: Novakoski's idea-maze filter requires an idea to sit at the intersection of three things — a large market, a mission the team is excited about, and something the team would beat competitors at building — and he says derivatives trading satisfies all three for Lighter.
insights.speaker: Vlad Novakoski
insights.so_what: A compact three-part screen investors can apply to founder pitches, with an explicit failure case attached.
insights.quote: want to build something that sits at the intersection of three things. One, like something that there's like a large market for, right? Another thing is a mission we're excited about.

insights.claim: Novakoski diagnoses Lunch Club's failure as a market-size error rather than an execution or product error: the networking market inflated during COVID and then shrank, and the business plateaued without dying.
insights.speaker: Vlad Novakoski
insights.so_what: COVID-era demand should be treated as a temporary market-size distortion, not a new baseline — a recurring underwriting error in 2020-2021 vintages.
insights.quote: where we got it wrong was the market was actually not very big like it got big during co and then shrunk.

insights.claim: Lunch Club's key implementation insight was avoiding adverse selection by removing double opt-in: unlike dating, networking under open requests floods a few famous people with unanswerable requests while high-potential unknowns get none, so the system assigns the match instead.
insights.speaker: Vlad Novakoski
insights.so_what: A generalizable design rule for any two-sided marketplace with heavily skewed desirability — user choice degrades match quality where attention is the scarce good.
insights.quote: the key insight on the implementation side was like how do we avoid adverse selection, right?

insights.claim: Peter Thiel's advice to Novakoski when he moved from finance to Silicon Valley was not to start a company yet but to first learn how startups work from inside one, advice Novakoski followed through Quora and Adapar before founding Lunch Club.
insights.speaker: Vlad Novakoski
insights.so_what: Counterweight to the drop-out-and-found narrative: domain and operating apprenticeship preceded both of his successful ventures.
insights.quote: his advice was like don't start a company yet like get to know how startups work first, right?

insights.claim: Novakoski cites Jensen Huang's rejection of five-year plans in favour of deciding what to do tomorrow as his own operating stance, saying Lighter plans one to two quarters ahead and lets customer feedback set direction.
insights.speaker: Vlad Novakoski
insights.so_what: Signals that Lighter's roadmap statements should be read as short-horizon commitments, not multi-year guidance.
insights.quote: I like what um you know Jensen has to say you know from Nvidia about how like you know we don't think about five year plans. We think about what we're going to do tomorrow.

insights.claim: Novakoski first read the Bitcoin whitepaper in 2012 only because an Olympiad friend showed it to him, and was drawn in because it applied number theory creatively — an illustration that his talent network functioned as his deal-flow and information-flow channel.
insights.speaker: Vlad Novakoski
insights.so_what: Early access to non-consensus ideas travelled through a closed peer network years before public awareness — the same channel that later produced his hiring edge.
insights.quote: the only reason I knew about it is because of a friend I made through Olympiads showed me the paper
